full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This Criminal appeal under section 28 of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 at the instance of Md Abdul Halim is directed against the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 22-7-2003 passed by the learned Judge, Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, Naogaon in Nari-o-Shishu Case No. 88 of 2002 convicting the appellant Md Abdul Halim under section 9(1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 and sentencing him to suffer imprisonment for life and also to pay a fine of Taka 5000 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for a period of 1(one) year more. 

 2. The prosecution case as stated in the FIR, in short, is that on 17-10-2001 corresponding to 2nd Kartik 1408 BS at about 11-00 at night the occurrence took place; that the accused had a rice mill situated at a distance of 150/200 cubits to the western side of the informant's house; that the accused used to look after the mill and stayed there; that the accused gave proposal to the informant Mst Umme Kulsum to marry her and also gave indecent proposals to her on several occasions while he passed through the nearby road but the informant did not give any response to the proposal; that on the date of the occurrence the informant slept in her room while her father and mother slept at the verandah of their room; that at about 11-00 at night the accused entered into her room cutting rope of the bamboo- made door and started committing rape upon her fastening her mouth; that the informant tried to free herself from that condition and raised scream, that hearing the scream her father and mother woke up; that then the informant caught the lungi of the accused but the accused left the place leaving his lungi, gamcha and torchlight thereon and that the victim identified the accused by the light of the torchlight. It is further stated that a salish took place when the matter was taken to the notice of local matabbar; that a proposal for marriage was given; that the accused disobeying decisions of shalish fled away; that then the informant lodged the petition of complaint with the local police station and thereafter the investigating officer after investigation submitted final report in favour of the accused stating the occurrence false. 

 4. During trial the prosecution in order to substantiate its case in all examined 5 witnesses out of whom PW 1 is the informant and alleged victim, PW 2 is the father of the informant, PW 3 and 4 are the maternal uncles of the informant, PW 5 is the sister of the informant. 

 7. The defence case as it transpires from the trend of cross-examination of the PWs and the suggestion put forward to them is the total denial. His case, infer alia, is that the proposal was given to the accused to marry the alleged victim and he was taken to the kazi office under a great influence and durance but the Kazi office did not register the marriage as the men of the accused side were not present and a quarrel took place regarding Kabinnama and at one stage the accused fled away from there. Thereafter the accused did not agree to marry her for which the informant party has implicated him in this false case. 

 8. In consideration of the evidence on record as well as the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Judge, Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Adalat, Naogaon, found the accused Abdul Halim guilty of the offence under section 9(1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 and convicted him there under and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life and also to pay a fine of Taka 5000 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for (one) year more. 

 10. Mr M Enayetur Rahim with Ms Shahida Begum, the learned Advocates for the appellant, took us through the final report, FIR, order sheet of taking cognisance, charge so framed and the deposition of the prosecution witnesses and the impugned judgment and order and material papers as available in the paper book and submits that this is a case of no evidence; that the prosecution witnesses are interested and closely related and that the learned trial Judge arrived at a decision on surmise and conjecture. He further submits that the learned trial Court failed to consider that the prosecution intentionally withheld the neighbouring witnesses; that the prosecution has come with some interested witnesses, who for obvious reasons corroborated the prosecution case; that the learned trial Court ought not to have relied upon such interested and biased witnesses. He further submits that the learned trial Court was manifestly wrong in convicting and sentencing the accused appellant without properly weighing and sifting the evidence on record and thus the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 11. The learned Deputy Attorney-General for the State opposes the appeal and submits that the prosecution proved its case against the accused appellant by the most consistent, corroborative and overwhelming evidence of competent witnesses and that the learned Judge of Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Adalat, Naogaon, was perfectly justified in convicting and sentencing the accused appellant on the basis of the most cogent and reliable evidence and his judgment does not suffer from any misreading and non-reading of evidence. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that all the prosecution witnesses are natural, probable and competent witnesses and there is no internal point of falsehood in their evidence on any point and, as such, the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Court. 

 13. To appreciate the illegality or impropriety of the impugned judgment, it is necessary to scrutinise the law and the evidence relating to the facts of the case. 

 15. PW 1, Umme Kulsum, is the informant and victim of the case. She deposed that the occurrence took place on 2nd Kartik, 1408 BS at 11-00 PM; that the accused had a rice mills situated at a distance of 150/200 cubits to the western side of the informant's house; that the accused used to look after the mills and stayed there; that the accused gave proposal to the informant Kulsum to marry her and sometimes he also gave her indecent proposals while he passed through the nearby road but the informant did not give any response to his proposal. 

 18. This witness further deposed that the investigating officer, without considering the case properly, filed final report and that she being aggrieved filed naraji petition against final report and the Court accepted the Naraji petition. She identified the Naraji petition marked Exhibit-2 and her signature therein is marked Exhibit 2/2. 

 21. She denied the defence suggestion that her father tried to marry her with the accused and that the accused was taken to the marriage registrar's office but he declined to marry her and that is why she filed this false case against the accused. 

 24. He denied the defence suggestion that no such occurrence as alleged had occurred; that the accused did not rape his daughter and that he has brought this false case for compelling the accused to marry his daughter. 

 26. In the cross-examination, he admitted that he and PW 4 are the maternal uncles of the victim and that the people nearby heard the occurrence but they are not witnesses in this case. 

 27. He denied the defence suggestion that this false case is brought for compelling the accused to marry the victim. 

 30. She denied the defence suggestion that this false case was brought only for compelling the accused to marry the victim. 

 31. From the scrutiny of the evidence discussed above it is admitted that all the PWs are closely related to each other and the prosecution failed to examine any independent and disinterested witness. The prosecution did not examine the most vital and relevant witnesses namely, the investigating officer of the case and the doctor who held the medical examination of the alleged victim. The Court below totally failed to consider the legal and factual implication of the report of the medical examination to consider the prosecution case as to whether the alleged victim was at all raped by the accused and in the said report, it was clearly stated that no sign of rape or violence was found. Non examination of neighboring witnesses namely Anower, Zillur Rahman and Shamsuddin and the members of salish namely Nazir, Saibor and Mujibur and non production of alamot like Lungi, Gamcha and Torchlight have made the prosecution case shaky and doubtful. The Court below failed to consider the defence case in its proper perspective with reference to the evidence on record, particularly the report of the medical examination and also failed to examine neighboring witnesses and members of salish and this failure has resulted in miscarriage of justice. 

 32. The alleged occurrence took place on 17-10-2001 and the alleged FIR was lodged long after 18 days that is on 5-11-2001 and no reasonable explanation of delay has been given in lodging the FIR which also clearly creates doubt about the story of the prosecution case. 

 33. The investigating officer of the case after holding proper investigation into the case submitted the police report on 5-11-2001 mentioning the alleged occurrence false and praying for taking legal steps against the alleged informant but the Court below rejecting the said police report illegally without showing any reason accepted the Naraji petition filed by the informant. Such whimsical rejection of final report and mechanical acceptance of Naraji petition has violated the established principle of law because there must be some reasons for rejection of final report and acceptance of Naraji petition. Such power of the Tribunal of rejection of final report and acceptance of Naraji petition is discretionary power of the Court which should be exercised judiciously not whimsically. Such whimsical exercise of discretionary power is always deprecated and discouraged. 

 34. The learned Judge approached the case in an emotional way rather without considering the legal evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case which has also resulted in miscarriage of justice in convicting the appellant. 

 35. The instant case is a case of no evidence and, as such, the learned Tribunal acted illegally in passing impugned judgment and order of conviction. The learned Tribunal passed the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence on mere surmises and conjectures as well as on misconception of law in pointing and connecting the circumstances against the appellant. The alleged allegation brought against the appellant does not at all come within the mischief of section 9(1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000. The prosecution case suffers from inherent absurdity and improbability and, as such, the learned Tribunal ought to have disbelieved the prosecution case and ought to have acquitted the appellant. 

 36. Examination of accused appellant under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure now may be addressed. Section 342 of the Code lays down for the purpose of enabling the accused person to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against him/he trial Judge shall after the examination of witnesses and before he is called on for his defence, afford opportunity to accused person to clear his mind. The fundamental principle underlying in section 342 of the Code is that the accused should be afforded a full and fair opportunity for explaining the evidence and circumstances against him. Thus need of law for examining the accused with reference to incriminating circumstances appearing against him in prosecution evidence is not for observance of a ritual in a trial nor is it mere formality. Section 342 of the Code is a mandatory provision for procedural law and a departure from fundamental principle of section 342 of the Code causes prejudice to the accused. This section confers a valuable right of the accused and at the same time gives an opportunity to the Court to administer justice. It is the bounden duty of the Court to question the accused properly to clear his mind as regard the charges against the accused and exact case in simple language is to be put to the accused so that the accused can meet each material point that is sought to be made against him and affording him a chance to meet and explain those incriminating circumstances and accusation if he can and so desires. The answers given by the accused during such examination ought to be considered by the Court. The principles in section 342 of the Code are the legislative guidelines for the Court to follow in toto. Court is to give due weight to answers of the accused, though it does not mean that such answer could be made the sole basis of any finding. The proper examination of the accused under section 342 of the Code will help to impart equitable justice. 

 37. In the instant case the learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to put the essence of testimonies of witnesses and incriminating evidence to the accused person. The provision contained in section 342 of the Code appears to have not been followed at all and the accused appellant had been highly prejudiced by impermissible examination under section 342 of the Code. 

 38. We received support of the above view in the case of State vs Sabir Miah reported in 11 BLT 294 = 8 BLC 235. 

 39. Considering the above facts, circumstances and evidence on record, one important question was brought before us as to how the learned Judge, Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, convicted the accused under section 9( 1) of the Ain and sentenced him there under to suffer imprisonment for life with fine dishonouring the final report and basing only on the evidence of highly interested witnesses. Is the learned Judge justified in taking cognisance of the case under section 9(1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 and what procedure he is to follow for taking cognisance of the offence under section 27(1) of the Ain, 2000. 

 40. It appears from the record that after filing the FIR on 5-11-2001 by the victim Umme Kulsum against the accused Abdul Halim that he raped her, the task of investigating the case was reposed to one SI Md Hafizur Rahman who after investigating the case submitted final report on the finding that it is false, concocted and planted case for compelling the accused Abdul Halim to marry victim Umme Kulsum. The Investigating Officer in the final report stated: 

 41. The case came to the learned Tribunal for decision as to final report. In the meantime the victim filed naraji petition. The learned Tribunal Judge fixed 28-4-2002 for taking decision on final report and Naraji petition. The learned Judge simply stated: 

 44. Now let us see the decision in this regard. In the case of Nurul Hoque vs Bazal Ahmed reported in 48 DLR 327, wherein it is stated: "The moot question in this case is, as to whether a Magistrate is competent to take cognisance of an offence in respect of an accused person on the basis of a naraji petition, although the accused person was previously discharged pursuant to a final report submitted by the police. The word "discharge" has not been defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure but nevertheless the word "discharge" connotes different meanings in different contexts. When an accused is discharged pursuant to a final report that means that the accused has been discharged from custody under section 500 of the Code and not dis- charged from the case. The legal position is, that a second prosecution is permissible if the order of discharge was not passed on merits. If cognisance is taken on the basis of a fresh complaint there can be no objection to the proceedings at all and in a proper case an application for revival also may amount to a fresh complaint. A naraji petition is a fresh complaint and a Magistrate is competent to take cognisance on the basis of a naraji petition by complying with the requirements of the Code. 

 45. It is also stated in the case of Shahjahan Ali Mondal vs Belayet Hossain reported in 47 DLR 478, wherein it is observed "Informant if feels aggrieved by the police report in the nature of a final report in favour of the accused persons may file a petition to such a Magistrate complaining against such a report. Such a petition is termed as naraji petition though there is no mention of such/naraji petition in the Code. It is now well settled that naraji petition is nothing but a petition of complaint under section 200 of the said Code and on receipt of such naraji petition Magistrate may take cognisance against such accused persons or may direct further investigation by the police. The magistrate is not bound by the final report and may take cognisance against the accused persons on consideration of materials on record or may direct further investigation on his own motion also." 

 46. It is stated in the case of Abu Bakkar vs State with Md Bazlur Rahman vs State reported in 1996 BLD 283 wherein it is stated: "The Magistrate is not bound to accept the report submitted by a police officer under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure recommending discharge of the accused, which is popularly known as a final report, if he finds that there are prima facie materials on record for proceeding against the accused persons. In such a case, a Magistrate is competent to take cognisance of the case under section 190(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 48. Analysing the above provisions of law and the decisions cited above on the subject, we are of the view that taking cognisance of offence disregarding the final report of police is an extra- ordinary power of the Tribunal. The Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal should exercise such extraordinary function very cautiously giving due importance to the established principles of law and the decisions taken in this regard. But in the instant case, the learned Tribunal disposed of the final report not on merit, but mechanically. The learned Tribunal took decisions in the following way. চুড়ান্ত রিপোর্ট অগ্রাহ্য করা হইল। নারাজী দরখাস্ত মঞ্জুর করা গেল। is now well established that naraji petition is nothing but a petition of complaint under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On receipt of such Naraji petition, the Tribunal may take cognisance against the accused if it is found reasonable and proper or direct further investigation by higher authority or by another agency of investigation. 

 49. In the instant case, the learned Tribunal neither perused the evidence on record properly nor did he follow the established principle of law and decision taken on the subject. Thus the learned Tribunal acted illegally in rejecting the final report and in accepting the naraji petition without appreciating the evidence on record which resulted in a miscarriage of justice, 

 50. The Court has to come to a decision on the basis of the evidence adduced before it by the parties. The Court is to see whether the findings of guilt of the accused is made out beyond reasonable doubt and then only conviction can be awarded. The governing principle is known as standard of proof does not exist. To determine the proof of a case beyond reasonable doubt is a very delicate task. A testimony without a fringe or embroidery of untruth is rare. The Court can reject it only when it is tainted to the core, that is where falsehood and truth are inextricably intertwined. If this is not so the Court must separate the grain from the chaff. Every piece of evidence has to be subjected to the test of objectivity. Fabric of truth should be the guiding factor. It is the duty of the Court to disengage the truth from falsehood. The Court has to assess the worth of necessarily imperfect human testimony. In a criminal case, the Court cannot proceed to consider the evidence of prosecution witnesses in a mechanical way. The broad features of the prosecution case, the probabilities and normal course of human conduct of the prudent person are some factors which are always kept in mind, while evaluating the merits of the case and fixed formula can be adapted. 

 51. In the light of above mentioned theory of assessing evidence for attaining decision, we, having given our anxious consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, find that the learned Tribunal did not follow the theory and has come to the decision in a mechanical way. 

 53. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 22-7-2003 passed by the learned Judge, Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, Naogaon in Nari-o-Shishu Case No. 88 of 2002 convicting the appellant Md Abdul Halim under section 9(1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 is set aside. Let the appellant Md Abdul Halim be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
